_comment: The ledger of DELIBERATE breaking changes to published contracts.
A maturity classification answers whether a change is allowed. This file answers whether
a change that has ALREADY happened was allowed, and records the evidence for it. Without
it, maturity is an opinion: the only way to find out whether a breaking change was
sanctioned is to read the git history and guess.
Every entry needs: the module, the SHA, what changed, and why the declared maturity
permits it. No task in the build enforces this file, so an entry that is incomplete, or that
names a module that is not published, is not caught automatically.
An entry is NOT permission to break anything silently. It is the receipt for a decision
that was taken deliberately. A reader cannot judge whether the decision was wise; the entry
can only show that it was made, written down, and attached to a SHA.

entries.change: added a third field `attempt: Int`, with NO default value
reasoning: This is a genuine binary break, not an additive one: the two-argument constructor,
component2, copy and copy$default all disappear from the ABI dump.
A default value of 0 would have made BCV accept it while leaving the defect in place,
because 0 names no control row and would be published as totalAttempts=0. The
alternative considered and rejected: keep the field out and let the engine derive the
attempt from a hash — which is exactly the fabrication this change removes, and
which crashed the engine with IllegalStateException before the fix.
The producer already had the real value: WaitUntilReconciler was iterating the attempt
and discarding it into a reason string. So this change does not invent a value, it
stops discarding one. The cost is paid by consumers constructing the class; there are
none outside this repository, which is the practical content of EXPERIMENTAL here.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a — additive field, no member removed

entries.change: property type `String` -> `FailureKind`; getFailureKind() descriptor changes on all three DSL entry points, and the JVM signature moves from Ljava/lang/String; to Ldev/rubentxu/pipeline/v2/domain/FailureKind;
reasoning: Two breaks, not one, and they are separate properties. BINARY: the descriptor changes, so
an artifact compiled against 0.47.0 calling getFailureKind() gets a NoSuchMethodError.
SOURCE: a pipeline that wrote error("boom", "USER") no longer compiles.
The alternative considered and rejected: keep a String overload alongside the typed one.
It would have preserved both breaks at the cost of the thing this migration exists to
remove — two spellings for one decision, only one of them checked. A typo in the String
overload would compile exactly as it did before, so the defect would survive behind a
compatibility shim. HARMONIC_COMPATIBILITY is the wrong word for a decision whose whole
problem was that it was unchecked.
The change also moves the published Gradle contract: pipeline-scripting-api now declares
api(project(":pipeline-domain")) instead of implementation(...). That is what writes the
dependency into the compile-scope variant of the published module metadata, and without it
a consumer cannot name FailureKind at all. Recorded here because it is part of what a
consumer resolves, not an internal build detail.
What did NOT change, and is why this is cheap for consumers: the wire. FailureKind.name is
the historical token of every case, so dsl-v1 payloads are byte-identical and durable
records written before this SHA still decode. The unknown-token refusal is unchanged too,
still an IllegalArgumentException at the decoder rather than a defaulted UNKNOWN.
The habituated authoring form is unchanged: error("msg") needs no import and no
vocabulary, because the default carries it. Only the explicit non-default case names the
type, which is the case where compile-time checking earns its import.
Proven from the outside, not asserted: examples/scripting-contract-consumer declares ONE
coordinate and never names pipeline-domain, so the publisher's metadata is the only route
by which FailureKind resolves. Reverting api to implementation makes that build fail with
'Cannot access class dev.rubentxu.pipeline.v2.domain.FailureKind'. That control was
executed, which is what makes this entry a receipt rather than a promise.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a — no member removed; this is a descriptor change, not a deletion

entries.change: property type `String` -> `CatchErrorBuildResult`; getBuildResult()/getStageResult() descriptors move from Ljava/lang/String; to Ldev/rubentxu/pipeline/v2/domain/CatchErrorBuildResult;, and the same substitution applies to <init>, component1/2, copy and copy$default
reasoning: A genuine binary break: an artifact compiled against 0.47.0 that calls getBuildResult()
receives a NoSuchMethodError, and one that constructs the overlay with Strings no longer
links.
The wire did NOT change, and that is the whole reason this was affordable. The overlay is
@Serializable and carries these fields as BARE JSON STRINGS, so the ADT declares its own
serializer rather than letting kotlinx derive one: the derived form would have emitted
{"type":"UNSTABLE"} and silently changed the shape of every dsl-v1 IR document. The
serializer here emits and consumes the plain string, so the IR bytes are identical.
wireToken is DECLARED per case rather than derived from .name. The cases are PascalCase
and the historical wire is UPPER_CASE, so a derived token would have been a silent
rewriting of every durable record the first time someone renamed a case.
What this bought is not elegance, it is the removal of a fabrication. This overlay is where
a MISSING stageResult used to become the string "UNSTABLE" via ?: "UNSTABLE", and
UNSTABLE is not a neutral placeholder: it means the run continues while FAILURE aborts it. A
record the decoder could not read therefore came back describing a different run than the
one that happened. The typed field cannot express that, because there is no way to build a
CatchErrorBuildResult out of nothing.
Proven rather than asserted: CatchErrorHistoricalDecodingTest reads the real fixture
fixtures/07-catch-error.out.json, captured 2026-09-10 when both fields were String, and
decodes its 23 records with today's code. Both historical CatchErrorTriggered records
FAILURE/FAILURE and UNSTABLE/UNSTABLE come back as the typed values, and a historical absent
buildResult decodes back to absence rather than to a token.
There are no consumers of this constructor outside this repository, which is the practical
content of EXPERIMENTAL here. Consumers construct events and inspect projections; they do
not build overlay IR by hand.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a — no member removed; this is a descriptor change, not a deletion

entries.change: property type `String` -> `CatchErrorBuildResult`; getBuildResult()/getStageResult() descriptors move from Ljava/lang/String; to Ldev/rubentxu/pipeline/v2/domain/CatchErrorBuildResult;, and the same substitution applies to <init>, component6/7, copy and copy$default
reasoning: Same descriptor change as the overlay, on the event, and the same wire guarantee:
EventJsonWriter projects .wireToken and JsonEventLog parses it back, with a token outside
the vocabulary refused instead of defaulted. An absent buildResult still travels as the
historical empty token, because ABSENT_ON_WIRE predates this migration and changing it
would invalidate every stored record that omitted a nullable field.
This is the surface where the type matters most, and the reason is the reader. This event is
what an external observer consumes to learn that a failure was caught and what it became.
A String here is a token that any producer can spell any way; an unreadable one used to
arrive as "UNSTABLE" and be indistinguishable from a deliberate one.
The alternative considered and rejected: keep String and validate at the consumer. That
moves the same check to N places, leaves the writer able to produce a value no reader can
accept, and is exactly the shape of defect this migration exists to delete.
The classification permits this only because the module is EXPERIMENTAL and because the
wire is frozen: durable history written before this SHA still decodes to the same typed
value. A STABLE module could not carry this entry.
CatchErrorResultWireCompatibilityTest pins the three tokens and the ABSENT representation
in both directions, and SemanticFieldAbsentIsMalformedTest keeps the required fields
entries.removal_boundary: n/a — no member removed; this is a descriptor change, not a deletion

entries.change: property type `String` -> `CatchErrorBuildResult`; getBuildResult()/getStageResult() descriptors move from Ljava/lang/String; to Ldev/rubentxu/pipeline/v2/domain/CatchErrorBuildResult;, and the same substitution applies to <init>, component1/2, copy and copy$default. The AUTHORING surface was NOT broken and is NOT recorded here: catchError(String, String, String, Function1) is still in the dump byte-identical, and error(String, String) was ADDED to PostStepsScope and BranchScope
reasoning: One semantic decision here has TWO surfaces, and this entry exists to make the difference
legible rather than to hide it.
The AUTHORING surface is what a DSL author writes: catchError(buildResult = "FAILURE",
stageResult = "UNSTABLE") { ... }. That spelling was PRESERVED, deprecado with
LFC1-007, and bridged at construction: a token outside the vocabulary is refused by
LegacyResultVocabulary.refuse() before the pipeline exists, so a typo dies at build time
instead of producing a run that says something false. No entry is recorded for it, because
nothing about it broke.
This entry covers the IR surface instead, the StepSpec.CatchError an author never names
directly: it is what the compiler emits and what a serializer reads. Nothing outside this
repository constructs it, and its previous String shape permitted a token that no reader
could accept.
Recording only this one is deliberate. An entry here is a receipt for a decision that was
taken, not a permission slip: registering the authoring surface as broken would be a lie
about what shipped, and would also make the next reader believe the bridge is removable
when its whole purpose is to survive until the declared removal boundary.
The typed overload is unambiguous BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by convention: it requires
buildResult with no default, and making it optional does not compile. That was measured, not
assumed.
Proven from outside: examples/scripting-contract-consumer compiles only this one coordinate
and its LegacyAuthoringCompatibilityTest exercises both spellings, proving they produce the
same durable tokens, and proving USR, FAILLURE, success, "Stable" and the empty string are
refused at construction. 9 legacy assertions plus 3 typed, all against the published
artifacts.
entries.removal_boundary: authoring surface: declared by LFC1-007, no removal boundary set by this entry; IR surface: n/a, no member removed

entries.change: added property `refusals: List<EventRecordRead.Undecodable>`; the three-argument <init>(List, EventCursor, boolean), copy(List, EventCursor, boolean) and copy$default all DISAPPEAR from the dump, and component4/getRefusals plus the four-argument copy and copy$default are added
reasoning: A genuine binary break, and the distinction that makes it one is worth stating precisely:
the default value on `refusals` buys SOURCE compatibility only. Kotlin emits the full
constructor plus a synthetic one taking a DefaultConstructorMarker, never the old
three-argument form, so an artifact compiled against 0.47.0 that constructs or copies an
EventPage receives a NoSuchMethodError. A consumer that REBUILDS against 0.48 links and
needs no source edit.
There is a real external consumer of this constructor, so the cost is not hypothetical:
examples/fabric-contract-consumer implements EventTail twice and constructs EventPage at
InMemoryPorts.kt:115 and PublishedReadSurfaceTest.kt:137. Both use named arguments and omit
`refusals`, which is exactly why the source survives the rebuild. What is NOT proven here,
and is not claimed, is a rebuild against 0.48: that consumer resolves against the published
0.47.0 artifacts today, and 0.48 is not cut yet. The source claim rests on reading the call
sites, not on a run.
The alternative considered and rejected: @JvmOverloads on the constructor, which would keep
the three-argument form in the ABI and make apiCheck pass with no entry at all. It would
publish a constructor meaning "a page with no refusals" — a supported way to build a page
that hides a history it has not read. That is the defect this field exists to remove,
re-published as a convenience overload, and paying for it with a silent lie is worse than
paying for it with a recorded entry.
What this buys: a durable row that exists and cannot be read now reaches the consumer. Before
this field the only way to express it was to throw the page away, so a consumer paging
history could not tell "there was nothing more" from "there was one more thing I could not
read", and the continuation — which advances by ROW — could never get past such a row. The
field's type is the store's own EventRecordRead.Undecodable rather than a page-side twin,
because a second refusal type would be a second authority, with the store naming one thing
and the page another.
EventQuery.matches, changed in the SAME block, is deliberately NOT recorded here. It is
purely additive: a new method, no member removed, no descriptor changed. Recording it would
be a lie about what shipped, in a ledger whose whole purpose is to be the opposite.
The module permits this because it is EXPERIMENTAL and because nothing about the DURABLE
WIRE changed: rows written before this SHA are read by exactly the same SQL cut and decode
to exactly the same typed values. A STABLE module could not carry this entry.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a — the three-argument <init>, copy and copy$default are removed by THIS entry and are not coming back; the four-argument forms are the contract from 0.48 onward

entries.change: THREE separate breaks in one commit, and they are listed separately because treating them as one would hide the only part a consumer has to act on. (1) PluginManifest: the constructor, copy and copy$default change arity and shape — schemaVersion:ManifestSchemaVersion, apiRange:PipelineKApiRange and contributions:PluginContributions are added, and getStepManifests() is REMOVED. (2) StepManifest: the class disappears from the dump entirely, replaced by PluginStepContribution with the same two members; the typealias StepManifest = PluginStepContribution keeps SOURCE compatibility for Kotlin callers and does nothing for a compiled caller. (3) PluginManifestValidator.validate: (PluginManifest, List) becomes (PluginManifest, List, Set, Set); the new parameters carry default values, which buys SOURCE compatibility and NO binary compatibility, since Kotlin emits the full four-argument form plus a synthetic one and never the old two-argument descriptor
reasoning: BINARY, in all three parts. An artifact compiled against 0.47.0 that constructs a PluginManifest, calls getStepManifests(), or calls the two-argument validate receives a NoSuchMethodError. A consumer that REBUILDS against 0.48 needs no source edit at all: the new fields are named, the two-argument validate still compiles through its defaults, and StepManifest resolves to the typealias. That difference is the whole reason this entry exists rather than a compatibility shim.

The alternative considered and rejected for each: keep StepManifest as a deprecated subclass, keep a two-argument validate overload, and keep a deprecated getStepManifests(). Together they would have made apiCheck pass with NO entry at all. What they would also have done is publish three ways to say the same thing, only one of which is checked — and the unchecked ones are exactly the ones a plugin author would keep reaching for, because they are the ones that still compile. A manifest is a DECLARATION whose whole value is being cross-checked against what the plugin actually provides; duplicating its vocabulary makes the unchecked spelling the convenient one, and the convenience is the defect. The cross-check only has force if there is exactly one thing to cross-check.

What this buys, stated as the defect it removes: before this SHA the manifest could not express which PipelineK versions it supports, so there was nothing for admission to refuse a plugin on. PluginManifestValidator ran INSIDE each plugin, which meant a plugin could forget to validate and nothing in the runtime would notice. And the duplicate declaration had nowhere to die — a manifest naming the same StepKey twice was not a contradiction that failed, it was a first-wins question that answered itself at registration time in whatever order the classpath happened to offer.

PluginContributions now refuses duplicates AT CONSTRUCTION, so a self-contradictory manifest cannot be built rather than merely being discouraged. families was KEPT and is not a second truth: it answers 'what domain is this plugin for' (SCM, NETWORK, TESTING) while contributions answers 'which structural shapes does it add', and neither derives from the other — a TESTING plugin contributes Steps, a NETWORK plugin contributes a Step plus a Capability.

Two defects were found while reviewing this change before committing it, and both are corrected in the SAME SHA, which is worth recording because both were laws that could not fail. First, the capability cross-check was tautological: every migrated plugin declared declaredCapabilities by READING contract.requiredCapabilities, and the validator compares declared == required, so the equality was guaranteed by construction and no mutation could ever turn it red. The per-Step capabilities are now declared as literals. Second, validateDirectives and validateEvents returned early when the supplied set was empty, so a manifest declaring a Directive or an Event that no contributor provides passed silently — precisely the negative mutant that must be refused. Both were caught by reading, not by a failing test, which is why they are named here rather than left as an unremarkable part of the diff.

This entry does NOT claim the work is finished, and the ledger is the wrong place to pretend otherwise. There is no machine-readable manifest inside the artifact yet: schemaVersion and apiRange exist in the domain, but no codec reads them from a JAR. PluginAdmission does not exist as a central authority: the validator is still called from inside each plugin, which is the inverted responsibility that the admission gate exists to fix. The manifest is a better declaration than it was; it is not yet an admission gate.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a — getStepManifests() and the StepManifest class are REMOVED by THIS entry and are not coming back; PluginStepContribution is the contract from 0.48 onward, reachable under the old name only as a Kotlin typealias

entries.change: removed the whole InMemoryStepRegistry class from the ABI, removed both register methods from the StepRegistry interface, and changed the receiver of the registerContributors extension from StepRegistry to StepRegistryBuilder; StepRegistryBuilder was added as the new composition type
reasoning: This is a genuine binary break and the measurement says so, unlike C/D/E where the
apiDump diff carried zero removals and registering an exception would have been a
false record of what was published.
StepRegistry's own KDoc already demanded the opposite of what the type allowed. It said
the registry was read-only after registration and that no mutation path existed, while
the interface carried two public register methods. Any holder of the reference could
extend the registry a reader was consulting, so the immutability was a convention. This
change makes it a property of the type: the interface has no registration method at all,
and StepRegistryBuilder is the only type that can register anything.
The alternative considered and rejected: keep register with @Deprecated. That would have
let apiCheck pass with no entry recorded here, while publishing two ways to compose —
only one of which would force composition to finish before observation. A deprecated
mutation path on a published registry is the exact shape this block exists to remove, and
a break recorded honestly is cheaper than a silent second authority.
InMemoryStepRegistry was deleted rather than deprecated for a second reason: it had no
reader that was not a test constructing a registry to register into, and keeping it would
have left a mutable StepRegistry implementation on the classpath of every consumer for a
migration nobody had asked for. pipeline-domain is EXPERIMENTAL, and an EXPERIMENTAL
module is exactly where this break is allowed.
The cut is provable rather than asserted: FArchE4b4 and StepRegistryTest were extended so
that re-adding a method named register to the interface fails the build, and so that
mutating the builder after build() does not reach a registry already handed out.
entries.removal_boundary: Consumption in this repository is complete: 104 test files and 26 production files migrated, and the only remaining references to InMemoryStepRegistry in the tree were three test NAMES that named the deleted class. The external blast radius is bounded by the maturity classification: every published module here is EXPERIMENTAL, so no CONSUMER_COMPATIBLE promise is being broken.

entries.change: moved register off the EventRegistry class onto a new nested EventRegistry.Builder, and added EventRegistry.builder(); EventRegistry.create() is retained and now returns an already-frozen EMPTY registry
reasoning: Same defect class as pipeline-domain, in the second registry: EventRegistry's KDoc said
the registry was read-only after registration, and it carried a public register. The
claim was false for exactly as long as that method existed.
register stays on the ABI, as EventRegistry.Builder.register, so a caller who wants to
compose has a method with the same name and signature; what disappears is the ability to
compose through a reference that readers already hold. create() is kept precisely so that
the three production call sites that wanted an empty registry keep working, and they now
receive a value that cannot grow afterwards.
The alternative considered and rejected: leave register in place and rely on discipline.
That is the same claim-as-comment that this entry records as having been false.
entries.removal_boundary: Three production call sites migrated (ExternalEventDefinitionDiscovery.compose and two EventRegistry.create() sites that needed no change because create() survives). Test call sites in pipeline-events and examples/fabric-contract-consumer migrated. The RegistrationOutcome return type is unchanged, so total rejection semantics are identical. pipeline-events is EXPERIMENTAL.

entries.change: THREE changes in one commit, listed separately because they are three different facts a consumer has to act on. (1) StepFinished: added property `outcome: String?`; the eight-argument <init>(String, String, long, Instant, int, int, String, String), copy and copy$default all DISAPPEAR from the dump, and component9/getOutcome plus the nine-argument forms are added. (2) StepFinishedTyped: added property `stepType: String`; the five-argument <init>, copy and copy$default disappear and the six-argument forms are added. (3) StepFinishedTyped.outcome: same descriptor (String) but a DIFFERENT MEANING - it carried the step's TYPE and now carries the step's VERDICT. The capability id was re-versioned for that reason: runtime.eventshape.v1 is DEPRECATED and runtime.eventshape.v2 is what this build delivers
reasoning: BINARY, in parts (1) and (2). An artifact compiled against 0.47.0 that constructs a StepFinished or a StepFinishedTyped receives a NoSuchMethodError. A consumer that REBUILDS against this build needs a source edit, and that is the point of the design: the field has NO default value, so every construction site has to say what it means.

The alternative considered and rejected: give `outcome` a default of null, or add @JvmOverloads. Kotlin emits the full constructor plus a synthetic one taking a DefaultConstructorMarker and never the old eight-argument descriptor, so a default buys SOURCE compatibility and NO binary compatibility - and @JvmOverloads would keep the old form in the ABI. That old form would mean 'a terminal event with no verdict', a supported way to build an event that says nothing about the step's result: exactly the silence this change exists to remove, republished as a convenient overload. The EventPage.refusals entry refused the same shortcut for the same reason.

Part (3) is not a break of the JVM signature at all, and that is precisely why it needs a capability id of its own. The field was a String before and it is a String now, so a consumer that was compiled against the old shape keeps linking and keeps reading - a step's TYPE where it expected a verdict. The old shape filled `outcome` with raw.stepType, under a field whose name promised a result: a consumer got a confident answer to a question nobody asked and no answer to the question it did ask. Nothing in the type says so, so nothing but a new id can say it.

What this buys, stated as the defect it removes: the step boundary emits the terminal event from a finally, so the terminal event of a FAILED step is emitted too. Before this SHA a consumer could not tell a failed step from a successful one without joining the terminal event with the separate failure event - by a step index that does not say which stage the failure belongs to. The reviewer of this product called it: 'the translator can claim a Step finished successfully without enough evidence'. Now the verdict travels with the event that ends the step, and the reader that serves `inspect`'s OUTCOME column reads it from there.

The wire did NOT change shape: the payload is a JSON TEXT column, so the new field needs no migration, and a row written before this SHA decodes to NO verdict - which is the honest reading, because that build published none. A consumer that needs to tell 'this build says unknown' from 'this build says nothing' negotiates events.stepoutcome.v1.

What is NOT recorded here: the domain change that gives StepOutcome its canonical wire token. That one is purely additive - a new method and a new companion - and recording it would be a lie about what shipped, in a ledger whose whole purpose is to be the opposite.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a - the eight-argument StepFinished <init>, copy and copy$default, and the five-argument StepFinishedTyped <init>, copy and copy$default, are removed by THIS entry and are not coming back; the nine- and six-argument forms are the contract from this build onward. runtime.eventshape.v1 stays announced and not delivered: its `outcome` meant something else, and a consumer that negotiated it has to move to runtime.eventshape.v2

entries.surface: StepFailed.stageIndex, and the subject of the envelope that carries it
entries.change: TWO changes in one commit, listed separately because they are two different facts a consumer has to act on. (1) StepFailed: added property `stageIndex: Int?`; the nine-argument <init>(String, String, long, Instant, int, String, String, FailureKind, String), copy and copy$default all DISAPPEAR from the dump, and component5/getStageIndex plus the ten-argument forms are added. (2) the envelope's subject for a failure that names its stage changes from the RUN resource to the STEP resource: the descriptor of `subject` does not change at all, and what it points at does. A consumer that groups the plane by subject sees the failure move from the run to the step it belongs to
reasoning: BINARY, in part (1). An artifact compiled against 0.47.0 that constructs a StepFailed receives a NoSuchMethodError. A consumer that REBUILDS against this build needs a source edit, and that is the point of the design: the field has NO default value, so every construction site has to say what it means, and a construction site that cannot say it has to say that it cannot.

The alternative considered and rejected: give `stageIndex` a default of null, or add @JvmOverloads. Kotlin emits the full constructor plus a synthetic one taking a DefaultConstructorMarker and never the old nine-argument descriptor, so a default buys SOURCE compatibility and NO binary compatibility - and @JvmOverloads would keep the old form in the ABI. That old form would mean 'a failure that belongs to no stage', a supported way to build a failure event that never says where it happened: exactly the silence this change exists to remove, republished as a convenient overload. The StepFinished.outcome entry refused the same shortcut for the same reason.

A default of 0 was refused for a second reason, and it is the one that matters: 0 is a stage. A failure in the FIRST stage and a failure whose stage nobody recorded are two different facts, and a default of 0 turns the second into the first. A consumer would then attribute failures to a stage that nobody said they belonged to, which is the same fabrication the field was added to remove - one level down.

Part (2) is not a break of the JVM signature at all, and that is precisely why it travels with the entry. The subject of an envelope says what the event is ABOUT, and a failure that names its stage is about that step. A consumer that compiled against the old behaviour keeps linking and keeps reading - a failure under the run instead of under the step - and nothing in the type says so.

What this buys, stated as the defect it removes: the failure event used to name the step and not the stage. The step index is the index INSIDE a stage, so the same index means a different step in each stage of the run, and the only way to learn the stage was to join the failure with another event by a key that was not unambiguous between stages. A consumer that attributed the failure to a stage had to read a second event to learn something the failure could have said itself. The reviewer of this product called it: 'No se debe resolver esta carencia suponiendo a que Stage pertenecio el fallo'.

The wire did NOT change shape: the payload is a JSON TEXT column, so the new field needs no migration, and a row written before this SHA decodes to NO stage - which is the honest reading, because that build published none. A consumer that needs to tell 'this build says unknown' from 'this build says nothing' negotiates events.failurestage.v1.

What is NOT recorded here: the capability id `events.failurestage.v1` and the law of the harness that this stage made correlatable. The id is a new name in a catalogue, not a change to a published surface, and the law lives in the harness, whose contract is the event plane and not the event class. Recording them would be a lie about what shipped, in a ledger whose whole purpose is to be the opposite.
entries.removal_boundary: n/a - the nine-argument StepFailed <init>, copy and copy$default are removed by THIS entry and are not coming back; the ten-argument form is the contract from this build onward

entries.change: REMOVED two cases from the sealed interface EventFollowRefusal. The class EventFollowRefusal$RetentionLost and the object EventFollowRefusal$Cancelled disappear from the dump, each with its <init>, copy, copy$default and component descriptors. The vocabulary keeps three cases, one for each refusal the read port can name, and the translation between the two vocabularies stays one-to-one. The capability id was re-versioned for that reason: events.follow.v2 is DEPRECATED (announced and NOT delivered) and events.follow.v3 is what this build delivers
reasoning: Neither case was EVER produced. A census over the whole tree - production and tests - finds no
construction of either one, and the sealed 0.62.0 artifact does not contain a producer either.
So this is not a change of behaviour: the runtime already answered with the three cases that
remain.
RetentionLost said the run's retention had lost its beginning. The event store keeps every row it
writes - there is no DELETE against the events table anywhere in the tree - so a cursor is only
ever behind the tail, and there is no beginning that can be lost. The vocabulary even said so in
its own KDoc, in a sentence that described the case as the way a lost retention was signalled.
Cancelled said a cancellation. The follow's own handle contract says the opposite: close is the
only cancellation path, it is idempotent, and cancellation is a local lifecycle operation rather
than a follow outcome. The case contradicted the contract it shipped in.
The cost of leaving them is paid by every consumer, forever: a case in a sealed type is a branch
in the consumer's when, and a branch for a fact that cannot arrive is a branch nobody can test.
Removing a case is SOURCE-breaking for a consumer that rebuilds - its exhaustive when no longer
compiles - and it is NOT binary-breaking for one that does not: no constructor disappears from
any artifact a consumer might have linked, and the removed cases were never instantiated, so the
runtime answer is byte-for-byte the same. The re-versioned id is how a consumer learns which
shape it negotiated.
The alternative considered and rejected: keeping the cases and documenting that nothing produces
them. That leaves the published contract advertising states the product cannot enter, and the
consumer still writes the branch.
entries.removal_boundary: the two removed cases are not coming back under these names. A future policy that RELEASES event rows would need a case with a new name and a new id, because the fact it would name - a beginning that no longer exists - is not the fact these two named. Cancellation, if it ever needs to reach a consumer as a fact, is a different fact with a different name

entries.change: REMOVED four cases from the sealed interface OutputRefusal: the classes OutputRefusal$Corrupt, OutputRefusal$RangeLostRetention and OutputRefusal$FollowCancelled, and the object OutputRefusal$Unavailable, each with its <init>, copy, copy$default and component descriptors. The companion constant OutputRefusal.CORRUPT_REASON_MAX_LEN disappears with the case that was its only user. The vocabulary keeps nine cases, every one of them produced by the output store. The capability id was re-versioned for that reason: output.follow.v1 is DEPRECATED (announced and NOT delivered) and output.follow.v2 is what this build delivers
reasoning: None of the four was EVER produced. The census over the whole tree finds no construction of any
of them, and the sealed 0.62.0 artifact does not contain one either. So this is not a change of
behaviour: the runtime already answered with the nine cases that remain.
Each of the four was a fact imported from a plane that could not produce it either. Corrupt said
'a row exists but its payload does not back it' - the language of ROWS, in a plane whose payloads
are the bytes a child process wrote. Nothing parses them, so nothing can find them unparseable,
and the integrity check this plane does have is the digest the reader computes. The plane whose
payloads ARE parsed is the event plane, and it already answers with its own vocabulary: a row
that does not decode is reported as an undecodable record inside the page.
RangeLostRetention was the read-side twin of RetentionGap, with the same three fields and the
same meaning: two public cases for one fact. Unavailable was the read-side copy of a fact the
prune side does produce. FollowCancelled said the consumer closed the follow handle: closing a
handle is a lifecycle operation of the consumer's own, and the follow's contract says the close
is idempotent - it is not a refusal of a read.
The cost of leaving them is paid by every consumer, forever: a case in a sealed type is a branch
in the consumer's when, and a branch for a fact that cannot arrive is a branch nobody can test.
Removing a case is SOURCE-breaking for a consumer that rebuilds - its exhaustive when no longer
compiles - and it is NOT binary-breaking for one that does not: no constructor disappears from
any artifact a consumer might have linked, and the removed cases were never instantiated, so the
runtime answer is byte-for-byte the same. The re-versioned id is how a consumer learns which
shape it negotiated.
The alternative considered and rejected: keeping the cases and documenting that nothing produces
them. That leaves the published contract advertising states the product cannot enter, and the
consumer still writes the branch. The other alternative - giving Corrupt a producer - was
rejected on the evidence: the output plane's frames log is repaired by the writer (it truncates
back to the last whole frame and re-frames the committed bytes), so a damaged log is a transient
state a reader waits out, not a durable fault, and a durable refusal would have been a lie.
entries.removal_boundary: the four removed cases are not coming back under these names. If the output plane ever gains a payload it parses, or a retention that releases part of a range rather than all of it, the fact it would name is a new case with a new name and a new id.
